To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the multiple scattering of randomly distributed surface plasmon modes in a 2D nanohole array can be used to create multiple-input and multiple-out optical switching devices.
the random scattering of SPPs can be exploited to control multiple-input and multiple output channels for optical-to-electronic signal transfer.
a disordered array of randomly positioned nanoholes can be used to control SPPs in order to realize a multiple-input and multiple- output (MIMO) plasmonic switching system.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a novel class of plasmonic nanostructures, which is based on the concept of multiple scattering of SPPs.
the design and development of plasmonic devices that are capable of manipulating light at the subwavelength scale.

the control of randomly scattered surface-plasmon-polaritons (S-SPPs) in a two-dimensional ( 2D ) disordered array of nano-holes on a thin gold film, for multiple-input and -output (MI-MO) plasmonic switching applications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this work demonstrates the feasibility of using a random scattering array of nanohole antennas as a plasmonic switching and routing device for multiple-input and output channels.
this study presents an on-chip optical-to-electronic interface that enables the transfer of optical information from a photodetector to an electronic circuit.
the use of random multiple scattering in a 2D disordered array of nanoantennas provides a new strategy for on-chip plasmoinc switching devices with multiple inputs and outputs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a plasmonic switching architecture that can deliver a large amount of optical information to an electronic platform with high efficiency and low crosstalk.

the multiple-input and multiple-out switching device based on random SPP scattering can potentially serve as an on-chip interconnection network to link multiple photonic components to a single electronic processor, thus significantly improving the overall computing performance.
the SPPs can be controlled and manipulated with high efficiency in disordered plasmonic systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the multiple scattering of SPPs can be utilized to enhance the performance of on-chip plasmic devices.

the multiple scattering of surface plasmon waves in a disordered array of holes can be used to achieve a high degree of spatial decorrelation, which can be exploited in the development of novel on-chip plamonic devices.

the random multiple scattering of SPPs can be utilized for the design of on-chip optical interconnects, which can provide an effective way to transfer information from the photonic to the electronic platforms.
